title: Value Categories and Perfect Forwarding
summary: Every expression has a **type** and a **value category**: lvalue, xvalue or prvalue. In a template, `T&&` is a **forwarding reference**: it binds to anything and records whether the argument was an lvalue or an rvalue. `std::forward<T>(x)` passes it on with that category intact, which is **perfect forwarding**.
markdown:
## Value categories, precisely [[7.05 Move Semantics]] used a two-way split into lvalues and rvalues. The standard uses three primary categories, defined by two independent properties: does the expression have **identity** (does it refer to a particular object), and may its resources be **moved from**? ```mermaid flowchart TD E["expression"] --> GL["glvalue
has identity"] E --> R["rvalue
may be moved from"] GL --> L["lvalue
x, *p, v[0], a call returning T&"] GL --> X["xvalue
std::move(x), a call returning T&&"] R --> X R --> PR["prvalue
42, x + 1, T{}, a call returning T"] ``` | Category | Identity | Movable | Examples | |---|---|---|---| | **lvalue** | Yes | No | `x`, `*p`, `v[0]`, a string literal | | **xvalue** ("expiring") | Yes | Yes | `std::move(x)`, `static_cast(x)` | | **prvalue** ("pure rvalue") | No | Yes | `42`, `x + 1`, `T{}`, `make()` | A value category is a property of an **expression**, not of an object or a type. The same object can be named by an lvalue expression (`x`) and by an xvalue expression (`std::move(x)`). > [!important] A named rvalue reference is an lvalue > ```cpp > void f(std::string&& s) > { > g(s); // s is a name, so this expression is an lvalue: g copies > g(std::move(s)); // an xvalue: g may move > } > ``` > The **type** of `s` is `std::string&&`. The **value category** of the expression `s` is lvalue, because it has a name and could be used again. This is what makes forwarding necessary. ## Forwarding references `T&&` has a special meaning when, and only when, `T` is a template parameter **deduced** from that very parameter. ```cpp template void wrapper(T&& arg); // forwarding reference: binds to anything void f(std::string&& s); // rvalue reference: binds to rvalues only auto&& x{ expression }; // also a forwarding reference ``` | Declaration | Kind | |---|---| | `template void f(T&&)` | Forwarding reference | | `auto&&` | Forwarding reference | | `void f(Widget&&)` | Rvalue reference: no deduction | | `template void f(const T&&)` | Rvalue reference: `const` disqualifies it | | `template void f(std::vector&&)` | Rvalue reference: not of the form `T&&` | ### Reference collapsing Two rules produce the behaviour. **A special deduction rule.** When an lvalue of type `A` is passed to `T&&`, `T` is deduced as `A&`. When an rvalue is passed, `T` is deduced as `A`. **Reference collapsing.** A reference to a reference, which can only arise through templates and aliases, collapses: ``` & & becomes & & && becomes & && & becomes & && && becomes && an lvalue reference anywhere wins ``` | Argument | `T` deduced as | `T&&` becomes | |---|---|---| | An lvalue `std::string` | `std::string&` | `std::string& &&`, which collapses to `std::string&` | | An rvalue `std::string` | `std::string` | `std::string&&` | So `T` itself **encodes** the argument's original value category. ## `std::forward` Inside `wrapper`, `arg` is a name and therefore an lvalue, whatever was passed. `std::forward(arg)` restores the original category by reading it back out of `T`. ```cpp #include #include #include void process(const std::string&) { std::cout << "copy\n"; } void process(std::string&&) { std::cout << "move\n"; } template void relay(T&& arg) { process(std::forward(arg)); } int main() { std::string name{ "Ann" }; relay(name); // copy relay(std::string{ "Bo" }); // move relay(std::move(name)); // move return 0; } ``` ```mermaid flowchart LR A["relay(name)
an lvalue"] --> F["T is std::string&
forward yields an lvalue"] --> C["process(const std::string&)"] B["relay(temporary)
an rvalue"] --> G["T is std::string
forward yields an rvalue"] --> M["process(std::string&&)"] ``` `std::forward(arg)` is `static_cast(arg)`. With `T` as `std::string&` it collapses to an lvalue reference; with `T` as `std::string` it is an rvalue reference. | | `std::move(x)` | `std::forward(x)` | |---|---|---| | Produces | Always an rvalue | An lvalue or an rvalue, as recorded in `T` | | Use with | An rvalue reference or object you are finished with | A forwarding reference | | Template argument | Deduced | Must be written explicitly | ## The standard use: wrapping construction ```cpp template std::unique_ptr make(Args&&... args) { return std::unique_ptr{ new T(std::forward(args)...) }; } ``` Each argument reaches `T`'s constructor exactly as the caller supplied it: lvalues are copied from, rvalues moved from, and nothing is copied in between. `std::make_unique`, `emplace_back` and the constructor of `std::thread` all work this way. ## `decltype` and `decltype(auto)` | Expression | Yields | |---|---| | `decltype(x)` where `x` is a name | The declared type of `x` | | `decltype((x))`, or any other lvalue expression of type `T` | `T&` | | `decltype(` an xvalue `)` | `T&&` | | `decltype(` a prvalue `)` | `T` | ```cpp int x{}; decltype(x) a{}; // int decltype((x)) b{ x }; // int&: the parentheses make it an expression, not a name ``` `auto` strips references and top-level `const`. `decltype(auto)` deduces with the `decltype` rules, preserving them. That is what a forwarding wrapper needs for its return type: ```cpp template decltype(auto) call(F&& f, Args&&... args) { return std::forward(f)(std::forward(args)...); } ``` If `f` returns a reference, so does `call`. `std::invoke(f, args...)` generalises the call itself to member function pointers and member data pointers. ## Pitfalls | Pitfall | Why | |---|---| | Forwarding the same argument twice | The first use may move from it | | Overloading on a forwarding reference | `template void f(T&&)` is an exact match for almost anything and beats `f(const Widget&)` for a non-const lvalue. Constrain it with a concept. | | A forwarding constructor | It can hijack copy construction from a non-const lvalue. Constrain it. | | `return (x);` under `decltype(auto)` | The parentheses make it `T&`: a reference to a local | ## Check yourself ```quiz ? When is `T&&` a forwarding reference? - Whenever it appears in a template - Whenever `T` is a class type + When `T` is deduced from that very parameter, or as `auto&&` - Only when it is passed to `std::forward` > In `template void f(T&& x)` it is a forwarding reference. In a member of `Box` where `T` is already fixed, `T&&` is a plain rvalue reference. ? What is `T` deduced as when an lvalue `int` is passed to a `T&&` parameter? - `int` + `int&` - `int&&` - `const int&` > For an lvalue, `T` becomes `int&`, and `int& &&` collapses to `int&`. For an rvalue, `T` is plain `int`. ? Why is a named rvalue reference an lvalue? + A value category belongs to an expression, and a name refers to an object that can be used again - Because the compiler converts all references to lvalue references - It is not; it stays an rvalue everywhere - Because rvalue references cannot have names > Inside the function, `x` can be used many times, so using its name is an lvalue expression. That is why you write `std::move(x)` or `std::forward(x)`. ? What is the difference between `std::move` and `std::forward`? - `std::move` copies; `std::forward` moves the object - They are the same - `std::forward` always produces an lvalue reference + `std::move` always gives an rvalue; `std::forward` keeps the caller's > `std::forward` restores the category the caller passed, which `T` recorded. `std::move` is unconditional. ```
ideas:
1. Write `relay` and log which overload runs for an lvalue, a const lvalue, a temporary and a `std::move`d object.
2. Write `make<T>(args...)` and use it for a class whose constructor prints whether it copied or moved.
3. Write a `timed(f, args...)` wrapper that forwards everything and prints how long the call took.

cards.a:
When `T` is deduced from that very parameter, or as `auto&&`

In `template <typename T> void f(T&& x)` it is a forwarding reference. In a member of `Box<T>` where `T` is already fixed, `T&&` is a plain rvalue reference.

cards.q: What is `T` deduced as when an lvalue `int` is passed to a `T&&` parameter?
cards.a:
`int&`

For an lvalue, `T` becomes `int&`, and `int& &&` collapses to `int&`. For an rvalue, `T` is plain `int`.

cards.q: Why is a named rvalue reference an lvalue?
cards.a:
A value category belongs to an expression, and a name refers to an object that can be used again

Inside the function, `x` can be used many times, so using its name is an lvalue expression. That is why you write `std::move(x)` or `std::forward<T>(x)`.

cards.q: What is the difference between `std::move` and `std::forward`?
cards.a:
`std::move` always gives an rvalue; `std::forward` keeps the caller's

`std::forward` restores the category the caller passed, which `T` recorded. `std::move` is unconditional.
